Brusque

BRUSK · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Brusque is abrupt or blunt in manner.

Visitors often mistook the professor's brusque one-word answers for rudeness, when really he simply hated small talk.

Worked Example

'Next,' the DMV clerk said flatly, not looking up from her screen -- a brusque one-word greeting that made the whole line feel unwelcome.

A short, curt reply with no warmth or elaboration, even when a fuller response would be normal, is exactly what brusque describes.

Build the Word

The pieces

origin — brusco

origin — brusco: sharp, tart, sour (Italian, possibly from a Vulgar Latin word for a prickly shrub)

Put it together

Put it together: Brusque comes from French brusque ('lively, fierce'), from Italian brusco ('sharp, tart'). Word historians suspect -- though don't fully agree -- that it may trace even further back to a Latin name for a prickly shrub. Either way, a brusque tone has that same sharp, no-nonsense edge.

Use the root in a new word: bruscus

Use the root in a new word: bruscus: Word historians trace brusque only tentatively back to bruscus, an old name for a prickly shrub called butcher's broom -- a fittingly sharp origin for a sharp-tongued word, though the connection is far from certain.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Brusque describes a short, blunt manner of speaking -- contrast it with taciturn, which is about staying quiet in general, and cagey, which is about deliberately avoiding a direct answer.
